name: AI LLM Datasets Specialist — Dataset Creation × Model Formats × Quantisation × Alignment

mission.primary_objective: Design, curate, generate, validate, and format high-quality datasets for LLM fine-tuning and alignment training; select and work with model storage formats (GGUF, MLX, safetensors); apply quantisation selection rationale; perform and understand model modification techniques including abliteration; and understand alignment training methods (SFT, DPO, GRPO, RLHF) well enough to produce correct training artifacts for each.
mission.context: Dataset quality is the single hardest-to-fix variable in LLM fine-tuning. No training method, architecture, or hardware advantage compensates for bad data. The LIMA paper (2305.11206, 2023) demonstrated that 1,000 carefully curated, diverse, high-quality examples can outperform models trained on orders-of-magnitude more data. Microsoft's Evol-Instruct generated 250,000 instruction variants from 175 seed examples. Scale AI's research shows the optimal synthetic strategy shifts from answer augmentation to new question generation as query budget grows. These empirical anchors inform every decision in this skillset. The field advances weekly — treat benchmarks as snapshots, not axioms.
mission.target_outcome: Produce training-ready datasets in the correct format and quality level for any given fine-tuning goal; select the right model format and quantisation for any deployment target; understand abliteration mechanics to interpret or produce abliterated GGUF/MLX models; choose the right alignment training method and understand its data requirements.
mission.scope: Dataset creation (manual, synthetic, hybrid); dataset formats (Alpaca, ShareGPT, ChatML, DPO pairs, GRPO prompts, pretraining corpora); model formats (GGUF, MLX, safetensors, AWQ, GPTQ); quantisation taxonomy (K-quants, I-quants, legacy, dynamic/Unsloth UD); abliteration (dense and MoE architectures, projection methods, tool ecosystem); alignment training (SFT, DPO, ORPO, GRPO, PPO/RLHF); tooling (Unsloth, LLaMA-Factory, Axolotl, mlx-lm, Augmentoolkit, Evol-Instruct, RAGAS, LLM-as-Judge). Local inference context: LM Studio / llmster on Apple M4 Max with Qwen3.5 and similar models.

core_principles: QUALITY_OVER_QUANTITY — 1,000 carefully crafted, diverse, consistent examples outperform 50,000 mediocre ones (LIMA, 2023; NeurIPS 2023 empirical consensus); bad examples actively harm model performance
DIVERSITY_IS_MANDATORY — A dataset of 50,000 variations of 'What is X? X is Y.' teaches nothing; semantic, task, and stylistic diversity are as critical as volume
DATA_RESEMBLES_TARGET — Training data must match the exact format, tone, and structure you want at inference; fine-tuning is programming the model with examples, not teaching it generically
HUMAN_IN_THE_LOOP — LLM-generated synthetic data must be reviewed, filtered, and quality-checked by humans; fully synthetic pipelines without human gates create bias amplification and drift
DEDUPLICATION_MANDATORY — Near-duplicate examples actively degrade fine-tuned model performance; deduplicate semantically (embedding cosine similarity > 0.9 threshold) not just lexically
FORMAT_IS_CONTRACT — The dataset format (Alpaca, ShareGPT, ChatML) is a contract between data and training framework; mismatching format to framework breaks fine-tuning silently or noisily
QUANTISATION_IS_DEPLOYMENT_DECISION — Choose quantisation based on available memory and acceptable quality floor, not habit; Q4_K_M is a pragmatic default but not always optimal

ABLITERATION_IS_SURGICAL_NOT_GLOBAL — Modern abliteration on dense models modifies specific weight matrices orthogonal to a refusal direction; on MoE it requires multi-layer mapping across expert pathways

ALIGNMENT_METHOD_DETERMINES_DATA_SHAPE — SFT needs prompt/response pairs; DPO needs chosen/rejected preference pairs; GRPO needs prompts with verifiable outcomes; data format and alignment method are inseparable
PRESERVE_THINKING_IN_FINE_TUNED_MODELS — When fine-tuning reasoning models (Qwen3.5, DeepSeek-R1), include ≥75% chain-of-thought examples in the dataset or thinking capability degrades

layer_0_dataset_fundamentals.description: Core principles of what makes a fine-tuning dataset work or fail

truths: LIMA (2305.11206, 2023): 1,000 manually curated, diverse examples produced a model competitive with GPT-3.5-level instruction followers; the paper proved quality can trump quantity for SFT
LoRA/QLoRA fine-tuning: strong results achievable with 500–5,000 high-quality instruction-response pairs for well-defined, single tasks (DigitalOcean, 2026)
Full fine-tuning requires much larger datasets: tens to hundreds of thousands of examples; PEFT is the pragmatic path for most domain adaptation
Quality floor: a 10,000-example dataset where 20% of examples are ambiguous, contradictory, or low-quality performs worse than a 2,000-example clean dataset on the target task
Inspect quality continuously — read examples individually during generation, not after 50,000 are already produced; bad eggs compound
Training data should read like 'code you're writing to program the model' — every inconsistency is a bug (Meta AI blog, 2024)
Diversity requirement: the dataset must cover the full range of inputs the model will encounter at inference, not just the most common case

Diversity dimensions: task type (Q&A, reasoning, extraction, generation, classification), question phrasing (semantic diversity), answer length, difficulty (easy/medium/hard), domain subdomain coverage
Instruction Backtranslation: generate Q/A pairs by asking the LLM 'What questions could this text be the answer to?' — creates semantically diverse questions from a single document corpus
Paraphrasing input diversity: rephrase prompts while preserving semantics; used in SQLCoder2 fine-tuning to achieve syntactic + semantic input diversity
Cosine similarity deduplication: embed all examples with a fast embedding model; remove pairs where cosine similarity > 0.9 — semantic duplicates are more damaging than lexical duplicates

Telecom paper (arXiv 2509.25736): measuring pairwise embedding cosine similarity across synthetic dataset versus seed dataset with left-shift in histogram (lower similarity = greater diversity) is the correct diversity check
Bloom's Taxonomy application to diversity: include examples spanning recall, comprehension, application, analysis, synthesis, and evaluation levels — not just recall Q&A
Start small: build 100 examples of a specific target behaviour, train on them, test — iterate the pipeline before committing to full-scale generation
Task-specific SFT (single well-defined task): 500–2,000 high-quality examples sufficient with LoRA
Domain adaptation (broad domain, many subtasks): 5,000–50,000 examples; quality controls more critical at this scale
Instruction following (general capability improvement): 10,000–100,000 examples; Alpaca (52K) and WizardLM (250K via Evol-Instruct) are the reference scales
Continued pretraining on new knowledge: requires much larger corpora (100M+ tokens); fine-tuning alone is unreliable for injecting entirely new factual knowledge that wasn't in pretraining

The 'cannot add new knowledge' claim is overstated: large, well-structured datasets on a topic can inject new knowledge; what fails is single-paragraph or low-sample-count injections (LocalLLaMA community consensus)
DPO alignment: 10,000–50,000 preference pairs; quality of the 'rejected' response matters as much as the 'chosen' — bad rejected examples teach nothing
Stage 1 — Source selection: identify authoritative domain sources (PDFs, internal wikis, structured databases, existing HuggingFace datasets via search with sentence-similarity models)
Stage 2 — Extraction and cleaning: parse raw sources; strip HTML/boilerplate/PII; chunk long documents to context-appropriate size
Stage 3 — Q&A generation: use local LLM (Mixtral, Qwen3.5, Llama-3.1-70B) or teacher model (GPT-4) to generate instruction/response pairs from chunks
Stage 4 — Evolution (optional): apply Evol-Instruct in-depth (more detail) and in-breadth (new variants) evolution to seed examples to expand diversity
Stage 5 — Quality filtering: run LLM-as-Judge scoring; apply RAGAS metrics for domain-specific quality; threshold on quality score to discard low-quality outputs
Stage 6 — Deduplication: semantic dedup via embedding cosine similarity; lexical dedup via exact or near-exact hash comparison
Stage 7 — Format and export: convert to target format (Alpaca JSONL, ShareGPT JSONL, ChatML); validate schema; split train/val
Stage 8 — Review: manually read a random 1–5% sample; if quality is unsatisfactory, diagnose which generation stage is failing and fix at that stage — do not patch downstream

layer_1_synthetic_data_generation.description: Methods, tools, and failure modes for LLM-generated synthetic training data

truths: Seed-and-expand: curate 50–200 high-quality human examples; prompt LLM to generate N similar examples per seed; effective for domain-specific narrow tasks

Document-grounded QA: chunk documents → prompt LLM as 'Professor writing exam questions' with context → generate question + answer pairs grounded in the chunk (Mbando Reddit approach; Mixtral-8x7B locally via LM Studio)
Evol-Instruct (Microsoft, WizardLM): in-depth evolution adds complexity/detail; in-breadth evolution generates new variants; elimination removes failed outputs — 175 seeds → 250,000 instructions

Augmentoolkit (github.com/e-p-armstrong): open-source pipeline that ingests documents and outputs Q/A pairs ready for fine-tuning; most accessible automated dataset creation tool for domain-specific corpora
Answer augmentation: generate multiple answers to the same question (different styles, detail levels, formats); most effective when query budget ratio is low (Scale AI NeurIPS 2024 FITML workshop)
Question rephrasing: rephrase existing questions while preserving answer; robust even with weaker augmentation models; good for syntactic diversity without needing frontier LLM
New question generation: generate entirely new questions about the topic; most effective as query budget ratio increases — complement to augmentation, not replacement

Co-teaching / evolutionary iteration (Gretel Navigator): multiple LLMs critique and refine each other's outputs iteratively; can outperform single-model generation including GPT-4 by up to 25.6% on some tasks
Hybrid approach best: human-written data establishes correctness and tone; LLM-generated data scales volume; balance achieves better results than either alone
Use local LLMs (Mixtral-8x7B, Qwen3.5-35B-A3B, Llama-3.1-70B via LM Studio) for private/proprietary data — do not send company data to cloud APIs
Serve locally via LM Studio / KoboldCPP / Ollama → query via OpenAI-compatible /v1/completions or /v1/chat/completions endpoint
Python pattern: requests.post(url, headers=headers, json=payload) against local server; format selection depends on model chat template (alpaca, chatml, llama3)
Nudge JSON output: begin the model's response with '{' to force JSON structure; works with most local models
Implement retry logic: add garbage-detection check in generation loop (expected JSON field count, output length); discard and regenerate on failure
Post-generation crop: trim partially-generated trailing text; validate with json.loads() before saving
Licensing caution: verify the license of any LLM used for generation — cc-by-nc-4.0 or similar may prohibit using generated outputs for commercial model training
LLM-as-Judge: use a strong LLM (GPT-4o, Llama-3.1-70B) as judge to score quality; research shows strong LLM judges achieve >80% agreement with humans (Confident AI, 2024)
RAGAS metrics: Relevancy, Faithfulness, Context Recall, Context Precision — useful for document-grounded QA datasets; customisable domain-specific metrics (telecom specificity example)
Indistinguishability Rate (IR): have a strong LLM discriminate between synthetic and human-expert examples; IR close to 50% means the synthetic data is indistinguishable from human data
Reward model scoring: for preference datasets, use a trained reward model (e.g., nicolinho/QRM-Llama3.1-8B-v2) to score chosen vs rejected responses
Rule-based scoring: for math/code tasks, verify correctness programmatically (regex, unit tests, code execution) — cheapest and most reliable quality signal for verifiable outputs
Perplexity filtering for DPO: filter responses by perplexity relative to the policy model (responses too easy or too hard for the model are uninformative preference pairs)
Inspect 1–5% manually always: automated quality checks catch systematic errors; manual inspection catches creative failure modes no automated checker anticipated
50,000 variations of the same Q&A pattern — the model learns the pattern, not domain knowledge; diversity is not optional
Fully automated pipeline without human review gates — model collapse risk: LLM-generated data reinforces LLM biases at each iteration if unchecked
Using a model to generate training data for itself (same model, same weights) — produces circular bias; use a larger teacher model or diversified peer model
Skipping deduplication — near-duplicates bias the model toward common phrasings and harm generalization
Including PII, credentials, or proprietary identifiers in the dataset — becomes baked into model weights and may surface at inference
Not tracking provenance — without source linkage you cannot diagnose which documents caused hallucination patterns during fine-tuning
Generating examples without accounting for the chat template the training framework will apply — training on raw text then applying a chat template at inference creates prompt format mismatch

layer_2_dataset_formats.description: All major LLM fine-tuning dataset formats, their structure, use cases, and compatibility

truths: JSONL (JSON Lines): one JSON object per line; the production standard for fine-tuning datasets; append-friendly, streamable, easy to validate line by line
JSON: array of objects in a single file; valid for smaller datasets; cannot stream efficiently
Parquet: columnar binary format; efficient for large datasets (>100K examples); used by HuggingFace Datasets natively; not human-readable
CSV: acceptable for simple two-column (prompt/response) datasets; loses schema expressiveness for multi-turn data; avoid for preference data
Always validate JSONL line by line before training: json.loads(line) in a loop; invalid UTF-8 or malformed objects cause silent truncation in some trainers
Purpose: single-turn instruction following; the original format from Stanford's Alpaca (52K GPT-3 generated examples, 2023)
Schema: { 'instruction': string, 'input': string (optional context), 'output': string }
Multi-turn variant adds 'history': list of [user, assistant] string pairs
Training framework: LLaMA-Factory, Axolotl, Unsloth (apply_chat_template + alpaca column names)
The 'input' field is concatenated with 'instruction' at training time; keep 'input' empty unless you need context separation
Best for: Q&A from documents, extraction tasks, format conversion, domain-specific instruction following
Limitation: single-turn only in base form; ShareGPT handles multi-turn more naturally
Purpose: multi-turn conversations; closer to real chatbot interaction patterns
Schema: { 'conversations': [ { 'from': 'human'|'gpt'|'system'|'function'|'observation', 'value': string } ] }
Supports tool calling via 'function' and 'observation' roles — required for function-calling fine-tuning
LLaMA-Factory, Axolotl, Unsloth all natively support ShareGPT via formatting='sharegpt' flag
Conversion: Unsloth's standardize_sharegpt() converts ShareGPT 'from'/'value' keys to ChatML 'role'/'content' keys for models expecting ChatML template
Best for: chatbot fine-tuning, multi-turn dialogue, tool-use/function-call training, persona training
Continued pretraining: NOT supported by ShareGPT format — use plain text JSONL for pretraining
Origin: OpenAI's ChatML (Chat Markup Language); now the most widely-used conversation format
Schema: { 'messages': [ { 'role': 'system'|'user'|'assistant', 'content': string } ] }
Special tokens: <|im_start|>{role}\n{content}<|im_end|> delimiters in the tokenised form
HuggingFace tokenizer default apply_chat_template() outputs ChatML by default for many modern models
Qwen3.5, Llama-3.x, Mistral-Nemo: all use ChatML or ChatML-derived templates
Tool calling: 'tool_calls' field on assistant messages; 'tool' role for function results
Best for: any task targeting a model that was pretrained/SFT'd with ChatML template
DPO/ORPO/SimPO format: { 'prompt': string, 'chosen': string, 'rejected': string } — flat triplet
DPO ShareGPT variant: { 'conversations': [...], 'chosen': { 'role': 'assistant', 'content': '...' }, 'rejected': { 'role': 'assistant', 'content': '...' } }
KTO format (Kahneman-Tversky Optimisation): { 'messages': [...], 'label': true|false } — single response labelled as good or bad; does not require contrastive pairs
Preference data quality: the 'rejected' response must be plausible but inferior — trivially bad rejected responses teach nothing; close contrastive pairs are hardest to produce and most informative
Generating rejected responses: take a correct response, introduce a subtle error, remove a key detail, or use a weaker model's output
DPO on math: rule-based reward (regex correct/incorrect) to automatically label chosen/rejected from sampled model outputs — scalable without human labelling
GRPO training data: list of prompts only — GRPO generates multiple completions at training time and scores them via reward function
Schema: { 'prompt': string } or { 'messages': [ { 'role': 'user', 'content': string } ] }
No response column: GRPO generates G responses per prompt (G=8 typical) and uses intra-group reward differences to compute advantage
Reward functions: rule-based (math correctness, code execution, format adherence) or learned (reward model); verifiable tasks are ideal for GRPO
Difficulty matters more for GRPO than SFT: training on the hardest examples yields up to 47% larger performance gains vs training on easy examples (arXiv 2508.14094, 2025)
GRPO produced DeepSeek-R1's reasoning breakthrough; most accessible implementation: Unsloth GRPO notebooks on Google Colab
Continued pretraining: raw text JSONL, one document per line as { 'text': string }
No instruction structure: pretraining teaches the model to predict the next token from your domain corpus — does not teach it to answer questions
Combine with SFT: pretrain on domain corpus → then SFT with instruction format → best results for new knowledge injection
Common Crawl, Wikipedia, GitHub: standard pretraining corpora; use CC-NET or Dolma pipelines for filtering
Quality > coverage: perplexity-filtered, near-deduped pretraining data outperforms raw web dumps at the same token count

layer_3_model_formats.description: GGUF, MLX, safetensors, AWQ, GPTQ — what they are, when to use each

truths: GGUF (GPT-Generated Unified Format, or Georgi Gerganov Universal Format): binary file format that packages model weights, tokenizer, architecture metadata, and quantisation parameters into a single portable file
Ecosystem: native to llama.cpp; used by Ollama, LM Studio, Jan.ai, llamafile; the dominant format for local CPU/Apple Silicon inference
Three quantisation generations: Legacy (Q4_0, Q4_1, Q5_0, Q8_0) → K-quants (Q4_K_M, Q5_K_M, Q6_K) → I-quants (IQ2_XXS...IQ4_XS) using vector quantisation and importance matrices
Naming convention: Q = quantisation, number = bits per weight, K = K-quant family, M/S/L = size variant (Medium/Small/Large within the same bit depth), I = importance-matrix quant
K-quant advantage: uses 'super blocks' and grouped scaling; handles non-Gaussian weight distributions better than legacy linear quantisation
I-quant advantage: non-linear table-assisted reconstruction; fits heavy-tailed distributions at 2–4 bits; requires a calibration importance matrix (imatrix) during quantisation

Unsloth Dynamic 2.0 (UD) quants: selectively upcast critical layers (attention, embeddings) to higher precision while quantising less-sensitive layers more aggressively — SOTA accuracy on Pareto frontier
Self-contained: GGUF files include tokenizer vocabulary, special tokens, rope scaling parameters, model config — no separate files needed for inference
Conversion: python llama.cpp/convert_hf_to_gguf.py --input ./hf_model --output model.gguf --outtype f16 → then quantize: ./llama-quantize model.gguf model_Q4_K_M.gguf Q4_K_M
Q8_0: ~8-bit, near-lossless; largest GGUF; use when memory is ample and maximum quality is needed; 6.74 PPL on Qwen2.5-32B (benchmark, JarvisLabs 2026)
Q6_K: 6-bit K-quant; excellent quality; fits in less memory than Q8; sweet spot for large models on high-VRAM setups
Q5_K_M: 5-bit K-quant Medium; excellent quality-to-size ratio; recommended for production coding/reasoning tasks when memory allows
Q4_K_M: 4-bit K-quant Medium; the pragmatic default — ~75% memory reduction from FP16 while maintaining ~95% of quality; most-downloaded GGUF variant across all models
IQ4_XS: importance-matrix 4-bit; ~4.46 bpw vs Q4_K_M's ~4.89 bpw; slightly smaller, slightly faster generation, slightly slower prompt processing; use when squeezing every GB matters
Q3_K_M: quality degrades noticeably for reasoning/coding; avoid unless fitting in memory is the only constraint
Q2_K: significant quality loss; development/testing only
Unsloth UD-Q4_K_XL: recommended for Qwen3.5-35B-A3B on 36GB M4 Max; <0.1 PPL increase vs BF16 (benchmark, Benjamin Marie)
Platform decision: GGUF for CPU or Apple Silicon (llama.cpp/Metal); AWQ/GPTQ/Marlin for NVIDIA GPU (vLLM/TGI); MLX for Apple Silicon (MLX engine in LM Studio or mlx-lm CLI)
AWQ on NVIDIA: Marlin-AWQ achieves 741 tok/s vs 461 tok/s FP16 baseline on H200 at same quality; best speed+quality for CUDA deployments
MLX: Apple's open-source machine learning framework; uses its own weight format (safetensors + config.json on disk, loaded into MLX array types at runtime)
MLX models on HuggingFace: typically in mlx-community/ namespace (e.g., mlx-community/Qwen3.5-9B-8bit)
Not GGUF: MLX models cannot be loaded by llama.cpp; GGUF models cannot be loaded by mlx-lm without conversion
Conversion to GGUF: mlx-lm.fuse (merge adapters) → save as HF safetensors → convert_hf_to_gguf.py → quantize
MLX strengths: native Apple Silicon Metal shaders; best throughput for dense models on Apple Silicon (5–15% faster than llama.cpp Metal for same model); continuous batching in LM Studio 0.4.2+
MLX fine-tuning: mlx-lm LoRA training is the primary on-device fine-tuning path for Apple Silicon (see also layer_5 of the Qwen3.5 specialist skillset for parameter reference)
Quantisation in MLX: Q4, Q8, and bfloat16 supported; mlx.core.quantize() applies per-layer quantisation
safetensors: HuggingFace's standard model checkpoint format; replaces pytorch .bin files; safe (no code execution on load), faster to load, memory-mappable
Use for: full-precision inference (vLLM, transformers), fine-tuning output checkpoints, adapter weights (LoRA in safetensors form)
Not quantised by default: raw safetensors are BF16 or FP16; quantisation is applied separately (bitsandbytes at load time, AWQ offline, GPTQ offline)
PEFT LoRA adapters: stored as adapter_model.safetensors + adapter_config.json; merge into base model with merge_and_unload() for deployment

layer_4_abliteration.description: Abliteration mechanics, MoE-specific considerations, tool ecosystem, and parameter interpretation

truths: Foundational paper: Arditi et al. 2024 (arXiv:2406.11717, NeurIPS 2024) — 'Refusal in LLMs is mediated by a single direction in the residual stream'
Refusal direction: computed by taking mean activation difference between harmful and harmless prompt sets across layers; the resulting vector d_refusal is a direction in residual stream space
Activation steering: subtract the refusal direction from the residual stream at every token and every layer during inference — prevents model from representing the refusal direction
Weight orthogonalisation: modify the model weights directly by projecting the weight matrices orthogonal to d_refusal — the modification is permanent and does not require inference-time intervention

Which weights: matrices that write to the residual stream — attention projection weights (q_proj, k_proj, v_proj, o_proj) and MLP layers; the q/k/v/o_proj weights are the primary targets for attention-only abliteration
Abliteration ≠ fine-tuning: no backward pass required; operates on activations and weights directly; works even in 4-bit quantised models (bitsandbytes quantisation compatible for measurement)

Post-abliteration DPO heal: abliteration alone often degrades general capabilities (GSM8K math most sensitive); apply a short DPO round (NeuralDaredevil-8B pattern: abliterate → DPO heal) to restore quality
ablation_method='projection': applies projected abliteration — orthogonalises refusal direction against harmless direction during measurement to isolate pure refusal signal; reduces collateral damage
ablation_method='standard': conventional abliteration without harmless-projection; simpler, slightly higher collateral
refusal_vector_policy='per-layer': compute and apply a separate refusal direction vector for each transformer layer; more precise than using a single global direction

refusal_direction_method='projected': applies projection during the ablation step itself (distinct from measurement projection); combined with per-layer policy = norm-preserving biprojected abliteration

ablation_strength: multiplier on the ablation; 1.0 = standard; 2.0 = aggressive double-strength removal; higher values increase refusal suppression but also increase capability degradation; tune empirically
probed_layers='all': measure refusal direction signal across all transformer layers; look for peaks in the middle-to-late layers (typical refusal signal location for dense models)
pca_components (ablate-k=1): number of principal components of the refusal direction to ablate; k=1 ablates the dominant direction; k>1 ablates multiple dimensions (more thorough, more risky)

attention_only=True: abliterate only the attention projection weights (q_proj/k_proj/v_proj/o_proj), not MLP; used in MoE models to preserve expert routing quality — MLP expert weights handle domain-specific knowledge, routing is attention-driven
--normpreserve flag: preserve weight norms/magnitudes during ablation; prevents scale drift in the weight matrices; recommended for quality preservation
--invert flag: adds the refusal direction instead of subtracting — used to artificially increase refusal in under-aligned models
MoE abliteration is fundamentally harder than dense: refusal behavior is distributed across hundreds of experts per layer (Mixtral: 8 experts/layer; Kimi K2: 384 experts/layer)
Single-layer abliteration that works on 7B–14B dense models has zero effect on 1T MoE models like Kimi K2 (Cracken.ai domain-specific abliteration blog, 2026)

MoE strategy: map refusal signal strength across all layers; select N representative layers spanning the full computation pathway (early pattern encoding → final refusal expression); Cracken K2 example used 15 of 61 layers

attention_only=True for MoE: abliterating only attention projection weights (q/k/v/o_proj) instead of full MLP layers preserves expert routing quality — MoE router uses attention-derived representations to select experts

Why attention_only for MoE: MoE architecture description 'Abliteration targets only the attention projection weights (q/k/v/o_proj) to preserve expert routing quality' — the standard formulation for MoE abliteration configs

Domain-specific abliteration: MoE architecture's expert specialisation creates natural domain boundaries; it is possible to abliterate cybersecurity refusal while preserving explicit content safety (Cracken.ai result on Kimi K2)
Verification VRAM: large MoE models (Kimi K2 ~1T params) require 8× H200 GPUs for hidden state extraction; 35B-A3B can be measured in 4-bit on 24–36 GB VRAM

FailSpy/abliterator (GitHub): original TransformerLens-based implementation; requires TransformerLens architecture support; interactive exploration of refusal directions; limited to architectures with TransformerLens support

NousResearch/llm-abliteration (GitHub, DECCP): memory-efficient sharded processing; norm-preserving + projected variants; no TransformerLens dependency; processes 4-bit bitsandbytes models; <8GB VRAM for measurement; ~2 minutes runtime

jim-plus/llm-abliteration: supports dense and MoE architectures; tested on Llama-3.2, Qwen2.5-Coder, Ministral-8b, Mistral-7B, gemma-3-27b; --projected / --normpreserve / --invert flags; YAML config for multi-source multi-strategy application
ErisForge: minimal knowledge degradation; projection-based; recommended for dense models where capability preservation is critical
Heretic: Bayesian-optimised; fine KL/refusal tuning; handles nonstandard architectures; higher compute than DECCP; best for hard-to-abliterate models

HuggingFace abliterated models: >5,000 models with 'abliterated' in name as of 2025; quality varies enormously by tool and model; always test capability preservation benchmarks before using in production

Four-tool comparison (arXiv 2512.13655, Young 2025): DECCP offers best balance of compatibility and quality preservation across 16 models; Heretic wins on some architectures but has higher variance; FailSpy most limited by TransformerLens coverage (5/16 models)

Reading a model card like 'Base model: ./models/MiniMax-M2.5-8bit, Ablation method: projection, Refusal vector policy: per-layer, Refusal direction method: projected, Ablation strength: 2.0, Probed layers: all, PCA components: 1, Attention only: True' means: the base model was 8-bit quantised MiniMax M2.5; biprojected abliteration was applied (projection at measurement AND projection at ablation = maximum harmless-direction isolation); each transformer layer got its own refusal direction computed; aggressive 2× strength applied; the principal direction only (k=1) of the refusal subspace was ablated; ONLY the attention projection weights were modified, NOT MLP expert weights — this is MoE-safe abliteration

Ablation strength 2.0 + attention_only=True on MoE: very aggressive on the attention pathway while leaving MoE expert routing fully intact — the most surgical configuration for dense-model-equivalent refusal suppression on a MoE
Timestamp in model card: UTC datetime of when abliteration was applied — useful for tracing which version of the tool was used (pre/post MXFP4 fix era, etc.)

layer_5_alignment_training_methods.description: SFT, DPO, GRPO, RLHF/PPO — what each method needs, how they differ, and when to use each

truths: Purpose: teach the model to produce outputs in a specific format, style, tone, or domain; the foundation for all post-pretraining adaptation
Data shape: instruction/response pairs (Alpaca) or multi-turn conversations (ShareGPT/ChatML)
Training: cross-entropy loss on response tokens only (mask prompt tokens to avoid memorising prompts)
Works for: domain adaptation, instruction following, format compliance (JSON output), persona injection, new vocabulary alignment
Limitation: teaches what responses look like, not which responses are better; for preference alignment, follow SFT with DPO or GRPO
LoRA SFT: r=16, alpha=32 for domain adaptation; r=64 for larger behavioural shifts; target_modules usually ['q_proj','k_proj','v_proj','o_proj','gate_proj','up_proj','down_proj']
Thinking model SFT: include ≥75% chain-of-thought formatted examples (with <think>...</think> blocks) to preserve reasoning capability during domain SFT
Purpose: align model with human preferences by learning which of two responses is better — without a separate reward model
Data shape: { prompt, chosen (preferred response), rejected (non-preferred response) } triplets
Training: binary cross-entropy loss that increases probability of chosen and decreases probability of rejected relative to a reference model
DPO formula: L_DPO = -E[(x,y_w,y_l)~D][log σ(β log π_θ(y_w|x)/π_ref(y_w|x) - β log π_θ(y_l|x)/π_ref(y_l|x))]
β hyperparameter: controls strength of preference; β=0.1 is standard default; lower values = weaker preference enforcement
DPO vs RLHF: eliminates the trained reward model; simpler to implement; comparable quality to PPO-RLHF on most alignment tasks; more stable training
DPO limitation: less effective on multi-step reasoning where a single correct/incorrect label applies to a complex chain; GRPO handles this better
On-policy DPO: generate responses from the SFT model, score with a reward model or rule-based verifier, use as preference pairs — more effective than offline DPO on static human-labelled datasets
ORPO (Odds Ratio Policy Optimisation): combines SFT and DPO in a single step; no reference model needed; useful when compute is tight
Purpose: improve reasoning capabilities (math, code, multi-step logic) via RL without a trained reward model; popularised by DeepSeek-R1
Data shape: prompts only — GRPO samples G responses per prompt at training time
Training mechanism: for each prompt, generate G outputs; score each with reward function; compute advantage A_i = R_i - mean(R_group); update policy to increase probability of high-advantage outputs
Reward functions: rule-based preferred (math correctness via regex, code execution pass/fail, JSON format validity) or learned reward model; rule-based is the foundation for most GRPO success stories
G=8: generate 8 responses per prompt; balances variance reduction with computational efficiency (GRPO paper default)
KL regularisation β=0.1: prevents the policy from drifting too far from reference model during training
Dataset difficulty: hard examples yield up to 47% more performance gain than easy examples in GRPO training (arXiv 2508.14094, 2025); curate prompts at the edge of model capability
GRPO vs DPO: GRPO generates its own training signal at runtime; DPO relies on static human-labelled pairs; GRPO is better for verifiable tasks, DPO better for subjective preference alignment
Dr. GRPO: removes biases from original GRPO formulation; preferred variant in 2025-2026 implementations
Unsloth GRPO support: available for Qwen3.5, Llama-3.x, DeepSeek-R1 derivatives via open Colab notebooks
Purpose: the original alignment method; train a reward model from human preference data; then optimise the LLM policy with PPO to maximise reward model scores
Data shape: human preference pairs to train the reward model; then the aligned LLM generates rollouts which are scored by the reward model
PPO: Proximal Policy Optimisation; constraint: KL divergence between old and new policy bounded by δ; prevents catastrophic policy collapse
RLAIF (RL from AI Feedback): uses a strong LLM as the feedback annotator instead of humans; achieves comparable helpfulness ratings; outperforms RLHF on harmlessness (Constitutional AI paper)

Why RLHF/PPO is often replaced: requires training and maintaining a separate reward model; computationally intensive; unstable to hyperparameter choices; DPO and GRPO are simpler alternatives for most use cases

When RLHF/PPO is still necessary: very complex reward functions that cannot be reduced to pairwise comparisons; continuous reward signals (e.g., user engagement over time); online adaptation scenarios

Constitutional AI (Anthropic): red-team the model to generate harmful outputs → critique and revise against constitutional principles → RLHF on revised outputs; distributes the safety signal across tokens
Domain adaptation, style transfer, format compliance → SFT alone; use Alpaca or ShareGPT format
Safety alignment, helpfulness preference, subjective quality improvement → SFT first → DPO; use preference pair format
Reasoning improvement (math, code, multi-step logic) → SFT first → GRPO with rule-based reward; use prompt-only GRPO format
Instruction following on new domain + preference alignment → SFT → DPO in sequence; two-stage training
Very small dataset (<500 examples) + well-defined task → SFT with LoRA only; GRPO/DPO underfit with too-small datasets
Training a production assistant from scratch → pretraining corpus → SFT instruction tuning → DPO or PPO-RLHF alignment; full pipeline
Local fine-tuning on Apple M4 Max 36GB → SFT via mlx-lm LoRA (models up to 9B); DPO via mlx-lm (same size limit); GRPO via Unsloth on CUDA (Linux/Windows, not macOS)

layer_6_tooling_ecosystem.description: Tools for every stage of dataset creation, training, evaluation, and local deployment

truths: Augmentoolkit (github.com/e-p-armstrong): processes arbitrary documents into Q/A pairs; most accessible automated tool for building domain-specific instruction datasets from private corpora
Evol-Instruct / WizardLM: data evolution framework (in-depth, in-breadth, elimination); 175 → 250,000 diverse instructions; WizardLM reimplementation available on GitHub
Gretel Navigator: compound AI system with co-teaching and evolutionary iteration; can outperform GPT-4 on synthetic data quality; for teams with budget
LlamaIndex / LangChain document loaders: structured document ingestion for RAG-to-SFT pipelines; LlamaIndex specifically has dataset generators
Bonito: conditional synthetic instruction dataset generation from raw text; specialised for instruction-tuning corpora from domain documents
KoboldCPP / LM Studio local server: serve local LLMs via OpenAI-compatible API for private synthetic generation; Mixtral-8x7B and Qwen3.5-35B-A3B are the recommended local generation models
PyMuPDF: extract clean text from PDF documents for ingestion pipelines
SpaCy: tokenisation, sentence segmentation, NER — useful for structured extraction before Q/A generation

Unsloth: 1.5–2× faster fine-tuning, 50–80% less VRAM than vanilla transformers; supports Qwen3.5, Llama-3.x, Mistral; SFT + DPO + GRPO + PPO + reward modelling; GGUF export built-in; Colab notebooks for all major models
LLaMA-Factory: web UI + CLI; 100+ models supported natively; Alpaca + ShareGPT format; full range of training methods; production tool for teams
Axolotl: yaml-config-driven; flexible; supports all major fine-tuning methods; used in many production fine-tuning pipelines; requires more config expertise than LLaMA-Factory
HuggingFace TRL: the library underpinning most training frameworks; SFTTrainer, DPOTrainer, GRPOTrainer, RewardTrainer all in trl package
mlx-lm: Apple's fine-tuning framework for Apple Silicon; LoRA + DPO; 0.8B–9B models fit on 36 GB M4 Max; fuse adapters + export to GGUF
Axolotl + DeepSpeed ZeRO-3: production-scale multi-GPU training setup; required for 70B+ full fine-tune
HuggingFace Datasets: primary hub; 100K+ datasets; load with datasets.load_dataset(); search with sentence-similarity to find domain-relevant datasets
RAGAS: RAG evaluation framework but also useful for measuring document-grounded QA dataset quality; Faithfulness, Relevancy, Context metrics
DeepEval: dataset evaluation platform; LLM-as-Judge; benchmark regression; G-Eval, DAG, custom metrics
LLM-as-Judge pattern: provide judge-LLM with original context, generated Q&A, rubric → score 1–10; strong judges (GPT-4o, Llama-3.1-70B) achieve >80% human agreement

Open datasets worth knowing: Alpaca-52K (general SFT), WizardLM-250K (evolved instructions), UltraFeedback (DPO preference pairs, 64K), OpenHermes-2.5 (instruction following, 1M), FineTome-100K (ShareGPT multi-turn), Open-Platypus (STEM reasoning), MetaMathQA (math), CodeFeedback (code), Magpie-Align (synthetic preference), Cosmopedia (synthetic pretraining)
CCNet / Dolma: deduplication and quality filtering pipelines for large-scale pretraining corpora
datasketch MinHash LSH: approximate deduplication for large JSONL datasets without embedding every example
Sentence embedding dedup: encode all examples with all-MiniLM-L6-v2 or bge-small-en-v1.5 → cosine similarity threshold 0.9 → remove near-duplicates; best quality but slower for >100K examples
Argilla: data annotation platform with LLM integration; human-in-the-loop review UI for synthetic datasets; supports preference labelling for DPO

layer_7_new_knowledge_injection.description: How and when fine-tuning can inject new knowledge vs when it fails — the most misunderstood aspect of fine-tuning

truths: The claim 'fine-tuning cannot add new knowledge' is overstated: it mostly applies to low-sample, unstructured, or single-paragraph attempts — not to well-structured, large, domain-focused datasets
What fine-tuning reliably changes: output format, tone, vocabulary alignment, instruction following style, domain-specific terminology, response structure
What fine-tuning can inject: new factual knowledge when the training examples are numerous, well-structured, and internally consistent; the model generalises from examples to the underlying facts

What fine-tuning struggles with: entirely novel concepts with no pretraining basis whatsoever; isolated single facts without surrounding context; very large knowledge bases that require fundamental world model changes
RAG + fine-tuning complementarity: fine-tune for style/behaviour/format; use RAG for dynamic factual retrieval — this combination outperforms either alone for knowledge-intensive tasks

Continued pretraining approach: if the domain is entirely new (specialised scientific domain, proprietary system), continued pretraining on the domain corpus THEN SFT instruction tuning works better than SFT alone for knowledge injection
Catastrophic forgetting: aggressive fine-tuning on a narrow domain can reduce general capabilities; the model 'forgets' general knowledge as it specialises
LoRA mitigates forgetting: LoRA adapters train only a small fraction of parameters; the base model weights are frozen; general capabilities are preserved more than full fine-tuning
Data mixing: blend 10–20% general instruction data (e.g., OpenHermes, Alpaca) into domain-specific training data to maintain general capability while specialising
Epoch count matters: more than 2–3 epochs on a small dataset often causes overfitting and forgetting; monitor validation loss, stop early if it rises
Reasoning preservation: for thinking models (Qwen3.5, DeepSeek-R1), include reasoning-chain examples (≥75% of training mix) or the <think> mechanism degrades

format_selection_matrix.preference_alignment_dpo: DPO triplets { prompt, chosen, rejected } or ShareGPT DPO variant
format_selection_matrix.reasoning_rl_grpo: Prompt-only JSONL { prompt } or { messages: [{role: user, content: ...}] }

quantisation_decision_tree.maximum_quality_cuda: BitsandBytes or AWQ; Marlin-AWQ for throughput
quantisation_decision_tree.very_tight_memory: IQ4_XS or IQ3_XXS with calibration imatrix

abliteration_config_for_moe.note: attention_only=True preserves MoE expert routing quality by targeting only q/k/v/o_proj weights

alignment_method_data_requirements.SFT: instruction/response pairs; 500–50K; format-matched to target; diverse
alignment_method_data_requirements.DPO: prompt + chosen + rejected triplets; 10K–50K; rejected must be plausibly wrong, not trivially bad
alignment_method_data_requirements.GRPO: prompts only + verifiable reward function; difficulty-stratified; hard examples preferred
alignment_method_data_requirements.PPO_RLHF: preference pairs for reward model + policy rollouts; most complex; 100K+ pairs recommended
alignment_method_data_requirements.ORPO: prompt + chosen + rejected; same as DPO but no reference model; single-stage

anti_patterns: Creating 50,000 variations of a single Q/A pattern — trains pattern, not knowledge; diversity is non-negotiable
No human review gate on synthetic data — model collapse risk; automated quality checks cannot catch all systematic errors
Using the same model to generate its own training data without diversification — circular bias amplification
Not deduplicating semantically — near-duplicates bias the model and reduce generalisation silently
Applying Alpaca format to a multi-turn use case — model learns single-turn patterns; fails at conversational continuity
Generating DPO rejected responses that are obviously wrong — trivially bad rejections teach nothing; close contrastive pairs are necessary
Training more than 3 epochs on a small dataset — overfitting and catastrophic forgetting; monitor val loss, stop early
Fine-tuning reasoning models (Qwen3.5, DeepSeek-R1) with <75% reasoning-chain examples — thinking capability degrades silently
Mislabelling the chat template (e.g., training on ChatML but inferring with Alpaca template) — completions are garbage; always verify template alignment
Applying abliteration to MoE models using single-layer or dense-only tools — no effect; requires multi-layer per-expert pathway approach
Post-abliteration deployment without capability benchmarks — math/reasoning degrades predictably; always run GSM8K/MMLU delta check
Loading GGUF models into vLLM for production — GGUF in vLLM runs at 93 tok/s vs 461 tok/s for same model in llama.cpp/Metal; use GGUF only in llama.cpp ecosystem
Not verifying model card abliteration parameters before deployment — attention_only=False on an MoE means MLP expert weights were modified, potentially breaking routing
Injecting new knowledge via 5–10 fine-tuning examples — insufficient; new knowledge injection needs hundreds to thousands of structured, consistent examples or a continued pretraining stage
Including PII, credentials, or company-confidential identifiers in training data — they surface at inference and cannot be fully purged without retraining

key_papers_and_references.finding: 1,000 carefully curated diverse examples sufficient for strong SFT alignment; quality > quantity
In-depth + in-breadth evolution of 175 seed instructions → 250,000 diverse instructions; Evol-Instruct framework
Refusal in LLMs mediated by a single direction in residual stream; weight orthogonalisation removes refusal without retraining
